title: What can you say about myo-inositol in your ads and on your site?
summary: The library gives no supported wording for myo-inositol, because no listed source supports one at a dose. Avoid wording that names or implies a disease, a drug or a treatment, such as "Treats PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome)".

wordings_to_avoid.why: Names a disease; the review read concerns PCOS.

wordings_to_avoid.wording: Lowers blood sugar or insulin resistance

evidence_gap: No listed source gives a use with a dose for myo-inositol. Health Canada's multi-vitamin/mineral monograph (dated 26 June 2026) lists inositol among its complementary ingredients (Table 4) and says no claim can be supported on them; its general 'source of' statements (section 4.1) cover only the vitamins and minerals in Tables 1 to 3. There is no ODS fact sheet among those read, FDA lists no health claim, and Regulation (EU) No 432/2012 has none.

evidence_strengths.strong: At least two listed sources support it independently at a comparable dose and form, and none disagrees.
evidence_strengths.moderate: One listed source supports it as an evidence-based use at that dose, and no listed source disagrees.
evidence_strengths.limited: The only support is traditional use, the sources disagree, or the source itself calls the evidence weak.

reasons_to_avoid.drug: names a drug or presents the product as one
reasons_to_avoid.treatment: promises to treat, cure or prevent a condition

disclaimer: Not legal advice. This guide shows the wording that published evidence supports at a daily dose, from the sources linked below; it is not a ruling on any claim. Your own product, its form and dose, and your own evidence still need to match the wording you use.
